case_info.scenario: A healthy 69-year-old man presented with a painful, progressively enlarging ulcer located on the left buccal mucosa, persisting for more than 1 month. No significant medical history and no other associated symptoms or contributory factors were identified. On clinical examination, a large ulcer in the buccal mucosa adjacent was observed to the third molar region. The ulcer was 3 × 2 cm, grayish-yellow and shallow in nature, had smooth, well-demarcated borders covered by a fibrinopurulent membrane, and was painful (Figure 1). The specimen was submitted for pathology with a provisional diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma. Although the patient had no underlying medical conditions, he reported using tirzepatide for weight loss over the past 6 months and an occupation involving long-term exposure to nitrous oxide. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography of the skull base to mid-thigh was done after the pathology report to rule out any evidence of tumor. Large focus of intensive fludeoxyglucose-18 uptake was noted in the left oral cavity with slight evidence of left maxillary bone erosion. No other mass lesions or invasive growth were noted elsewhere.
case_info.caption: Clinical image of the ulcer in the left buccal mucosa. The ulcer was present for 1 month, covered by a grayish-yellow fibrinopurulent membrane, and was painful.
case_info.explanation: B. Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer The given condition was diagnosed as Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer (EBVMCU). The ulcer was a localized, shallow, well-defined mass covered with a fibrinopurulent membrane. In contrast, oral squamous cell carcinoma typically presents with nonhomogeneous, nodulo-proliferative, warty ulcers. Ulcers caused by deep fungal infections often appear irregular and necrotic and may be deeper or multifocal. Oral lymphomas, often associated with EBV, may present with ulceration but are generally accompanied by other symptoms, such as swelling and lymphadenopathy, and typically do not resolve quickly. EBVMCU was first described by Dojcinov et al1as a lymphoproliferative disorder presenting as a sharply defined cutaneous or mucosal ulcer, often associated with immunosuppression (autoimmune medication, posttransplant therapy, age-related immunosenescence, HIV infection).2To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of EBVMCU associated with immunosuppression possibly related to tirzepatide use. Histological analysis revealed ulcerated epithelium with extensive necrosis and fibrinopurulent exudate in the underlying connective tissue. Clusters of large atypical lymphoid cells with Hodgkinlike features were observed. Patchy fibrino-hemorrhagic necrosis and focal angioinvasion were present. A diffuse polymorphous infiltrate of intermediate-sized immunoblasts, epithelioid histiocytes, and large pleomorphic Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS)–like cells were noted. These cells showed strong positivity for EBER in situ hybridization, PAX5, CD3, CD20, and CD30 (Figure 2). The histological differential diagnoses include EBV-positive lymphoproliferative disorders, such as classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) and aggressive EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). EBVMCU can be distinguished by its polymorphous infiltrate, CD45-positive HRS-like cells, and lack of systemic involvement. EBVMCU is EBER positive, but unlike DLBCL, this positivity is generally restricted to B cells within the ulcer. Additionally, CD45 positivity in HRS-like cells helps differentiate EBVMCU from cHL.3,4The etiology of EBVMCU is not fully understood, but immunosuppression and advanced age are the primary risk factors. Dojcinov et al1reported 9 cases related to immunosuppressive medication (eg, azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclosporine A) and 17 cases related to age-related immunosenescence. Cases in immunocompetent individuals have also been described. One hypothesis suggests that mucosal trauma may lead to persistent stimulation and activation of B-lymphocytes, resulting in transformation due to EBV persistence. Impaired EBV-specific cytotoxic T-cell response may allow for unchecked B-cell and natural killer/T-cell proliferation.2 Tirzepatide, used for weight loss and type 2 diabetes, is associated with gastrointestinal tract adverse effects, including nausea, vomiting, and reduced appetite. In this case, such effects may have contributed to transient immunosuppression, leading to EBVMCU.5The patient also reported occupational nitrous oxide exposure. Studies have shown that long-term nitrous oxide inhalation showed significantly higher levels of interferon-γ and IL-4 concentrations. Although not validated clinically, long-term nitrous oxide inhalation has been shown to alter immune function markers, potentially contributing to subclinical immunosuppression.6 Following discontinuation of tirzepatide, the ulcer showed progressive healing within 1 month. Oncology consultation led to supportive treatment for EBVMCU, and there has been no evidence of disease recurrence at 6-month follow-up. Early diagnosis of EBVMCU is crucial to distinguish it from aggressive lymphoproliferative malignant neoplasms and to avoid unnecessary treatments. EBVMCU generally follows an indolent course and may resolve spontaneously or with minimal intervention.7In contrast, cHL, oral lymphomas, and DLBCL require intensive therapy. A thorough clinical history—including immunosuppressive medications or immune-modulating agents, like tirzepatide—plays a key role in diagnosis. While symptom resolution followed drug cessation in this case, further research is needed to explore a definitive causal relationship.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.

            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.

            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

1. Mental Demand

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.

2. Performance

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task

   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the

   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an

case_info.caption: Clinical image of the ulcer in the left buccal mucosa. The ulcer was present for 1 month, covered by a grayish-yellow fibrinopurulent membrane, and was painful.
case_info.explanation: B. Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer The given condition was diagnosed as Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer (EBVMCU). The ulcer was a localized, shallow, well-defined mass covered with a fibrinopurulent membrane. In contrast, oral squamous cell carcinoma typically presents with nonhomogeneous, nodulo-proliferative, warty ulcers. Ulcers caused by deep fungal infections often appear irregular and necrotic and may be deeper or multifocal. Oral lymphomas, often associated with EBV, may present with ulceration but are generally accompanied by other symptoms, such as swelling and lymphadenopathy, and typically do not resolve quickly. EBVMCU was first described by Dojcinov et al1as a lymphoproliferative disorder presenting as a sharply defined cutaneous or mucosal ulcer, often associated with immunosuppression (autoimmune medication, posttransplant therapy, age-related immunosenescence, HIV infection).2To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of EBVMCU associated with immunosuppression possibly related to tirzepatide use. Histological analysis revealed ulcerated epithelium with extensive necrosis and fibrinopurulent exudate in the underlying connective tissue. Clusters of large atypical lymphoid cells with Hodgkinlike features were observed. Patchy fibrino-hemorrhagic necrosis and focal angioinvasion were present. A diffuse polymorphous infiltrate of intermediate-sized immunoblasts, epithelioid histiocytes, and large pleomorphic Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS)–like cells were noted. These cells showed strong positivity for EBER in situ hybridization, PAX5, CD3, CD20, and CD30 (Figure 2). The histological differential diagnoses include EBV-positive lymphoproliferative disorders, such as classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) and aggressive EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). EBVMCU can be distinguished by its polymorphous infiltrate, CD45-positive HRS-like cells, and lack of systemic involvement. EBVMCU is EBER positive, but unlike DLBCL, this positivity is generally restricted to B cells within the ulcer. Additionally, CD45 positivity in HRS-like cells helps differentiate EBVMCU from cHL.3,4The etiology of EBVMCU is not fully understood, but immunosuppression and advanced age are the primary risk factors. Dojcinov et al1reported 9 cases related to immunosuppressive medication (eg, azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclosporine A) and 17 cases related to age-related immunosenescence. Cases in immunocompetent individuals have also been described. One hypothesis suggests that mucosal trauma may lead to persistent stimulation and activation of B-lymphocytes, resulting in transformation due to EBV persistence. Impaired EBV-specific cytotoxic T-cell response may allow for unchecked B-cell and natural killer/T-cell proliferation.2 Tirzepatide, used for weight loss and type 2 diabetes, is associated with gastrointestinal tract adverse effects, including nausea, vomiting, and reduced appetite. In this case, such effects may have contributed to transient immunosuppression, leading to EBVMCU.5The patient also reported occupational nitrous oxide exposure. Studies have shown that long-term nitrous oxide inhalation showed significantly higher levels of interferon-γ and IL-4 concentrations. Although not validated clinically, long-term nitrous oxide inhalation has been shown to alter immune function markers, potentially contributing to subclinical immunosuppression.6 Following discontinuation of tirzepatide, the ulcer showed progressive healing within 1 month. Oncology consultation led to supportive treatment for EBVMCU, and there has been no evidence of disease recurrence at 6-month follow-up. Early diagnosis of EBVMCU is crucial to distinguish it from aggressive lymphoproliferative malignant neoplasms and to avoid unnecessary treatments. EBVMCU generally follows an indolent course and may resolve spontaneously or with minimal intervention.7In contrast, cHL, oral lymphomas, and DLBCL require intensive therapy. A thorough clinical history—including immunosuppressive medications or immune-modulating agents, like tirzepatide—plays a key role in diagnosis. While symptom resolution followed drug cessation in this case, further research is needed to explore a definitive causal relationship.

case_info.explanation: B. Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer The given condition was diagnosed as Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer (EBVMCU). The ulcer was a localized, shallow, well-defined mass covered with a fibrinopurulent membrane. In contrast, oral squamous cell carcinoma typically presents with nonhomogeneous, nodulo-proliferative, warty ulcers. Ulcers caused by deep fungal infections often appear irregular and necrotic and may be deeper or multifocal. Oral lymphomas, often associated with EBV, may present with ulceration but are generally accompanied by other symptoms, such as swelling and lymphadenopathy, and typically do not resolve quickly. EBVMCU was first described by Dojcinov et al1as a lymphoproliferative disorder presenting as a sharply defined cutaneous or mucosal ulcer, often associated with immunosuppression (autoimmune medication, posttransplant therapy, age-related immunosenescence, HIV infection).2To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of EBVMCU associated with immunosuppression possibly related to tirzepatide use. Histological analysis revealed ulcerated epithelium with extensive necrosis and fibrinopurulent exudate in the underlying connective tissue. Clusters of large atypical lymphoid cells with Hodgkinlike features were observed. Patchy fibrino-hemorrhagic necrosis and focal angioinvasion were present. A diffuse polymorphous infiltrate of intermediate-sized immunoblasts, epithelioid histiocytes, and large pleomorphic Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS)–like cells were noted. These cells showed strong positivity for EBER in situ hybridization, PAX5, CD3, CD20, and CD30 (Figure 2). The histological differential diagnoses include EBV-positive lymphoproliferative disorders, such as classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) and aggressive EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). EBVMCU can be distinguished by its polymorphous infiltrate, CD45-positive HRS-like cells, and lack of systemic involvement. EBVMCU is EBER positive, but unlike DLBCL, this positivity is generally restricted to B cells within the ulcer. Additionally, CD45 positivity in HRS-like cells helps differentiate EBVMCU from cHL.3,4The etiology of EBVMCU is not fully understood, but immunosuppression and advanced age are the primary risk factors. Dojcinov et al1reported 9 cases related to immunosuppressive medication (eg, azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclosporine A) and 17 cases related to age-related immunosenescence. Cases in immunocompetent individuals have also been described. One hypothesis suggests that mucosal trauma may lead to persistent stimulation and activation of B-lymphocytes, resulting in transformation due to EBV persistence. Impaired EBV-specific cytotoxic T-cell response may allow for unchecked B-cell and natural killer/T-cell proliferation.2 Tirzepatide, used for weight loss and type 2 diabetes, is associated with gastrointestinal tract adverse effects, including nausea, vomiting, and reduced appetite. In this case, such effects may have contributed to transient immunosuppression, leading to EBVMCU.5The patient also reported occupational nitrous oxide exposure. Studies have shown that long-term nitrous oxide inhalation showed significantly higher levels of interferon-γ and IL-4 concentrations. Although not validated clinically, long-term nitrous oxide inhalation has been shown to alter immune function markers, potentially contributing to subclinical immunosuppression.6 Following discontinuation of tirzepatide, the ulcer showed progressive healing within 1 month. Oncology consultation led to supportive treatment for EBVMCU, and there has been no evidence of disease recurrence at 6-month follow-up. Early diagnosis of EBVMCU is crucial to distinguish it from aggressive lymphoproliferative malignant neoplasms and to avoid unnecessary treatments. EBVMCU generally follows an indolent course and may resolve spontaneously or with minimal intervention.7In contrast, cHL, oral lymphomas, and DLBCL require intensive therapy. A thorough clinical history—including immunosuppressive medications or immune-modulating agents, like tirzepatide—plays a key role in diagnosis. While symptom resolution followed drug cessation in this case, further research is needed to explore a definitive causal relationship.

Although the patient had no underlying medical conditions, he reported using tirzepatide for weight loss over the past 6 months and an occupation involving long-term exposure to nitrous oxide. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography of the skull base to mid-thigh was done after the pathology report to rule out any evidence of tumor. case_info.explanation: B. Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer The given condition was diagnosed as Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer (EBVMCU). The ulcer was a localized, shallow, well-defined mass covered with a fibrinopurulent membrane. In contrast, oral squamous cell carcinoma typically presents with nonhomogeneous, nodulo-proliferative, warty ulcers. Ulcers caused by deep fungal infections often appear irregular and necrotic and may be deeper or multifocal. Oral lymphomas, often associated with EBV, may present with ulceration but are generally accompanied by other symptoms, such as swelling and lymphadenopathy, and typically do not resolve quickly. EBVMCU was first described by Dojcinov et al1as a lymphoproliferative disorder presenting as a sharply defined cutaneous or mucosal ulcer, often associated with immunosuppression (autoimmune medication, posttransplant therapy, age-related immunosenescence, HIV infection).2To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of EBVMCU associated with immunosuppression possibly related to tirzepatide use. Histological analysis revealed ulcerated epithelium with extensive necrosis and fibrinopurulent exudate in the underlying connective tissue. Clusters of large atypical lymphoid cells with Hodgkinlike features were observed. Patchy fibrino-hemorrhagic necrosis and focal angioinvasion were present. A diffuse polymorphous infiltrate of intermediate-sized immunoblasts, epithelioid histiocytes, and large pleomorphic Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS)–like cells were noted. These cells showed strong positivity for EBER in situ hybridization, PAX5, CD3, CD20, and CD30 (Figure 2). The histological differential diagnoses include EBV-positive lymphoproliferative disorders, such as classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) and aggressive EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). EBVMCU can be distinguished by its polymorphous infiltrate, CD45-positive HRS-like cells, and lack of systemic involvement. EBVMCU is EBER positive, but unlike DLBCL, this positivity is generally restricted to B cells within the ulcer. Additionally, CD45 positivity in HRS-like cells helps differentiate EBVMCU from cHL.3,4The etiology of EBVMCU is not fully understood, but immunosuppression and advanced age are the primary risk factors. Dojcinov et al1reported 9 cases related to immunosuppressive medication (eg, azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclosporine A) and 17 cases related to age-related immunosenescence. Cases in immunocompetent individuals have also been described. One hypothesis suggests that mucosal trauma may lead to persistent stimulation and activation of B-lymphocytes, resulting in transformation due to EBV persistence. Impaired EBV-specific cytotoxic T-cell response may allow for unchecked B-cell and natural killer/T-cell proliferation.2 Tirzepatide, used for weight loss and type 2 diabetes, is associated with gastrointestinal tract adverse effects, including nausea, vomiting, and reduced appetite. In this case, such effects may have contributed to transient immunosuppression, leading to EBVMCU.5The patient also reported occupational nitrous oxide exposure. Studies have shown that long-term nitrous oxide inhalation showed significantly higher levels of interferon-γ and IL-4 concentrations. Although not validated clinically, long-term nitrous oxide inhalation has been shown to alter immune function markers, potentially contributing to subclinical immunosuppression.6 Following discontinuation of tirzepatide, the ulcer showed progressive healing within 1 month. Oncology consultation led to supportive treatment for EBVMCU, and there has been no evidence of disease recurrence at 6-month follow-up. Early diagnosis of EBVMCU is crucial to distinguish it from aggressive lymphoproliferative malignant neoplasms and to avoid unnecessary treatments. EBVMCU generally follows an indolent course and may resolve spontaneously or with minimal intervention.7In contrast, cHL, oral lymphomas, and DLBCL require intensive therapy. A thorough clinical history—including immunosuppressive medications or immune-modulating agents, like tirzepatide—plays a key role in diagnosis. While symptom resolution followed drug cessation in this case, further research is needed to explore a definitive causal relationship.

case_info.explanation: B. Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer The given condition was diagnosed as Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer (EBVMCU). The ulcer was a localized, shallow, well-defined mass covered with a fibrinopurulent membrane. In contrast, oral squamous cell carcinoma typically presents with nonhomogeneous, nodulo-proliferative, warty ulcers. Ulcers caused by deep fungal infections often appear irregular and necrotic and may be deeper or multifocal. Oral lymphomas, often associated with EBV, may present with ulceration but are generally accompanied by other symptoms, such as swelling and lymphadenopathy, and typically do not resolve quickly. EBVMCU was first described by Dojcinov et al1as a lymphoproliferative disorder presenting as a sharply defined cutaneous or mucosal ulcer, often associated with immunosuppression (autoimmune medication, posttransplant therapy, age-related immunosenescence, HIV infection).2To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of EBVMCU associated with immunosuppression possibly related to tirzepatide use. Histological analysis revealed ulcerated epithelium with extensive necrosis and fibrinopurulent exudate in the underlying connective tissue. Clusters of large atypical lymphoid cells with Hodgkinlike features were observed. Patchy fibrino-hemorrhagic necrosis and focal angioinvasion were present. A diffuse polymorphous infiltrate of intermediate-sized immunoblasts, epithelioid histiocytes, and large pleomorphic Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS)–like cells were noted. These cells showed strong positivity for EBER in situ hybridization, PAX5, CD3, CD20, and CD30 (Figure 2). The histological differential diagnoses include EBV-positive lymphoproliferative disorders, such as classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) and aggressive EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). EBVMCU can be distinguished by its polymorphous infiltrate, CD45-positive HRS-like cells, and lack of systemic involvement. EBVMCU is EBER positive, but unlike DLBCL, this positivity is generally restricted to B cells within the ulcer. Additionally, CD45 positivity in HRS-like cells helps differentiate EBVMCU from cHL.3,4The etiology of EBVMCU is not fully understood, but immunosuppression and advanced age are the primary risk factors. Dojcinov et al1reported 9 cases related to immunosuppressive medication (eg, azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclosporine A) and 17 cases related to age-related immunosenescence. Cases in immunocompetent individuals have also been described. One hypothesis suggests that mucosal trauma may lead to persistent stimulation and activation of B-lymphocytes, resulting in transformation due to EBV persistence. Impaired EBV-specific cytotoxic T-cell response may allow for unchecked B-cell and natural killer/T-cell proliferation.2 Tirzepatide, used for weight loss and type 2 diabetes, is associated with gastrointestinal tract adverse effects, including nausea, vomiting, and reduced appetite. In this case, such effects may have contributed to transient immunosuppression, leading to EBVMCU.5The patient also reported occupational nitrous oxide exposure. Studies have shown that long-term nitrous oxide inhalation showed significantly higher levels of interferon-γ and IL-4 concentrations. Although not validated clinically, long-term nitrous oxide inhalation has been shown to alter immune function markers, potentially contributing to subclinical immunosuppression.6 Following discontinuation of tirzepatide, the ulcer showed progressive healing within 1 month. Oncology consultation led to supportive treatment for EBVMCU, and there has been no evidence of disease recurrence at 6-month follow-up. Early diagnosis of EBVMCU is crucial to distinguish it from aggressive lymphoproliferative malignant neoplasms and to avoid unnecessary treatments. EBVMCU generally follows an indolent course and may resolve spontaneously or with minimal intervention.7In contrast, cHL, oral lymphomas, and DLBCL require intensive therapy. A thorough clinical history—including immunosuppressive medications or immune-modulating agents, like tirzepatide—plays a key role in diagnosis. While symptom resolution followed drug cessation in this case, further research is needed to explore a definitive causal relationship.

case_info.explanation: B. Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer The given condition was diagnosed as Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer (EBVMCU). The ulcer was a localized, shallow, well-defined mass covered with a fibrinopurulent membrane. In contrast, oral squamous cell carcinoma typically presents with nonhomogeneous, nodulo-proliferative, warty ulcers. Ulcers caused by deep fungal infections often appear irregular and necrotic and may be deeper or multifocal. Oral lymphomas, often associated with EBV, may present with ulceration but are generally accompanied by other symptoms, such as swelling and lymphadenopathy, and typically do not resolve quickly. EBVMCU was first described by Dojcinov et al1as a lymphoproliferative disorder presenting as a sharply defined cutaneous or mucosal ulcer, often associated with immunosuppression (autoimmune medication, posttransplant therapy, age-related immunosenescence, HIV infection).2To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of EBVMCU associated with immunosuppression possibly related to tirzepatide use. Histological analysis revealed ulcerated epithelium with extensive necrosis and fibrinopurulent exudate in the underlying connective tissue. Clusters of large atypical lymphoid cells with Hodgkinlike features were observed. Patchy fibrino-hemorrhagic necrosis and focal angioinvasion were present. A diffuse polymorphous infiltrate of intermediate-sized immunoblasts, epithelioid histiocytes, and large pleomorphic Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS)–like cells were noted. These cells showed strong positivity for EBER in situ hybridization, PAX5, CD3, CD20, and CD30 (Figure 2). The histological differential diagnoses include EBV-positive lymphoproliferative disorders, such as classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) and aggressive EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). EBVMCU can be distinguished by its polymorphous infiltrate, CD45-positive HRS-like cells, and lack of systemic involvement. EBVMCU is EBER positive, but unlike DLBCL, this positivity is generally restricted to B cells within the ulcer. Additionally, CD45 positivity in HRS-like cells helps differentiate EBVMCU from cHL.3,4The etiology of EBVMCU is not fully understood, but immunosuppression and advanced age are the primary risk factors. Dojcinov et al1reported 9 cases related to immunosuppressive medication (eg, azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclosporine A) and 17 cases related to age-related immunosenescence. Cases in immunocompetent individuals have also been described. One hypothesis suggests that mucosal trauma may lead to persistent stimulation and activation of B-lymphocytes, resulting in transformation due to EBV persistence. Impaired EBV-specific cytotoxic T-cell response may allow for unchecked B-cell and natural killer/T-cell proliferation.2 Tirzepatide, used for weight loss and type 2 diabetes, is associated with gastrointestinal tract adverse effects, including nausea, vomiting, and reduced appetite. In this case, such effects may have contributed to transient immunosuppression, leading to EBVMCU.5The patient also reported occupational nitrous oxide exposure. Studies have shown that long-term nitrous oxide inhalation showed significantly higher levels of interferon-γ and IL-4 concentrations. Although not validated clinically, long-term nitrous oxide inhalation has been shown to alter immune function markers, potentially contributing to subclinical immunosuppression.6 Following discontinuation of tirzepatide, the ulcer showed progressive healing within 1 month. Oncology consultation led to supportive treatment for EBVMCU, and there has been no evidence of disease recurrence at 6-month follow-up. Early diagnosis of EBVMCU is crucial to distinguish it from aggressive lymphoproliferative malignant neoplasms and to avoid unnecessary treatments. EBVMCU generally follows an indolent course and may resolve spontaneously or with minimal intervention.7In contrast, cHL, oral lymphomas, and DLBCL require intensive therapy. A thorough clinical history—including immunosuppressive medications or immune-modulating agents, like tirzepatide—plays a key role in diagnosis. While symptom resolution followed drug cessation in this case, further research is needed to explore a definitive causal relationship.

case_info.explanation: B. Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer The given condition was diagnosed as Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer (EBVMCU). The ulcer was a localized, shallow, well-defined mass covered with a fibrinopurulent membrane. In contrast, oral squamous cell carcinoma typically presents with nonhomogeneous, nodulo-proliferative, warty ulcers. Ulcers caused by deep fungal infections often appear irregular and necrotic and may be deeper or multifocal. Oral lymphomas, often associated with EBV, may present with ulceration but are generally accompanied by other symptoms, such as swelling and lymphadenopathy, and typically do not resolve quickly. EBVMCU was first described by Dojcinov et al1as a lymphoproliferative disorder presenting as a sharply defined cutaneous or mucosal ulcer, often associated with immunosuppression (autoimmune medication, posttransplant therapy, age-related immunosenescence, HIV infection).2To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of EBVMCU associated with immunosuppression possibly related to tirzepatide use. Histological analysis revealed ulcerated epithelium with extensive necrosis and fibrinopurulent exudate in the underlying connective tissue. Clusters of large atypical lymphoid cells with Hodgkinlike features were observed. Patchy fibrino-hemorrhagic necrosis and focal angioinvasion were present. A diffuse polymorphous infiltrate of intermediate-sized immunoblasts, epithelioid histiocytes, and large pleomorphic Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS)–like cells were noted. These cells showed strong positivity for EBER in situ hybridization, PAX5, CD3, CD20, and CD30 (Figure 2). The histological differential diagnoses include EBV-positive lymphoproliferative disorders, such as classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) and aggressive EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). EBVMCU can be distinguished by its polymorphous infiltrate, CD45-positive HRS-like cells, and lack of systemic involvement. EBVMCU is EBER positive, but unlike DLBCL, this positivity is generally restricted to B cells within the ulcer. Additionally, CD45 positivity in HRS-like cells helps differentiate EBVMCU from cHL.3,4The etiology of EBVMCU is not fully understood, but immunosuppression and advanced age are the primary risk factors. Dojcinov et al1reported 9 cases related to immunosuppressive medication (eg, azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclosporine A) and 17 cases related to age-related immunosenescence. Cases in immunocompetent individuals have also been described. One hypothesis suggests that mucosal trauma may lead to persistent stimulation and activation of B-lymphocytes, resulting in transformation due to EBV persistence. Impaired EBV-specific cytotoxic T-cell response may allow for unchecked B-cell and natural killer/T-cell proliferation.2 Tirzepatide, used for weight loss and type 2 diabetes, is associated with gastrointestinal tract adverse effects, including nausea, vomiting, and reduced appetite. In this case, such effects may have contributed to transient immunosuppression, leading to EBVMCU.5The patient also reported occupational nitrous oxide exposure. Studies have shown that long-term nitrous oxide inhalation showed significantly higher levels of interferon-γ and IL-4 concentrations. Although not validated clinically, long-term nitrous oxide inhalation has been shown to alter immune function markers, potentially contributing to subclinical immunosuppression.6 Following discontinuation of tirzepatide, the ulcer showed progressive healing within 1 month. Oncology consultation led to supportive treatment for EBVMCU, and there has been no evidence of disease recurrence at 6-month follow-up. Early diagnosis of EBVMCU is crucial to distinguish it from aggressive lymphoproliferative malignant neoplasms and to avoid unnecessary treatments. EBVMCU generally follows an indolent course and may resolve spontaneously or with minimal intervention.7In contrast, cHL, oral lymphomas, and DLBCL require intensive therapy. A thorough clinical history—including immunosuppressive medications or immune-modulating agents, like tirzepatide—plays a key role in diagnosis. While symptom resolution followed drug cessation in this case, further research is needed to explore a definitive causal relationship.

case_info.explanation: B. Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer The given condition was diagnosed as Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer (EBVMCU). The ulcer was a localized, shallow, well-defined mass covered with a fibrinopurulent membrane. In contrast, oral squamous cell carcinoma typically presents with nonhomogeneous, nodulo-proliferative, warty ulcers. Ulcers caused by deep fungal infections often appear irregular and necrotic and may be deeper or multifocal. Oral lymphomas, often associated with EBV, may present with ulceration but are generally accompanied by other symptoms, such as swelling and lymphadenopathy, and typically do not resolve quickly. EBVMCU was first described by Dojcinov et al1as a lymphoproliferative disorder presenting as a sharply defined cutaneous or mucosal ulcer, often associated with immunosuppression (autoimmune medication, posttransplant therapy, age-related immunosenescence, HIV infection).2To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of EBVMCU associated with immunosuppression possibly related to tirzepatide use. Histological analysis revealed ulcerated epithelium with extensive necrosis and fibrinopurulent exudate in the underlying connective tissue. Clusters of large atypical lymphoid cells with Hodgkinlike features were observed. Patchy fibrino-hemorrhagic necrosis and focal angioinvasion were present. A diffuse polymorphous infiltrate of intermediate-sized immunoblasts, epithelioid histiocytes, and large pleomorphic Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS)–like cells were noted. These cells showed strong positivity for EBER in situ hybridization, PAX5, CD3, CD20, and CD30 (Figure 2). The histological differential diagnoses include EBV-positive lymphoproliferative disorders, such as classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) and aggressive EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). EBVMCU can be distinguished by its polymorphous infiltrate, CD45-positive HRS-like cells, and lack of systemic involvement. EBVMCU is EBER positive, but unlike DLBCL, this positivity is generally restricted to B cells within the ulcer. Additionally, CD45 positivity in HRS-like cells helps differentiate EBVMCU from cHL.3,4The etiology of EBVMCU is not fully understood, but immunosuppression and advanced age are the primary risk factors. Dojcinov et al1reported 9 cases related to immunosuppressive medication (eg, azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclosporine A) and 17 cases related to age-related immunosenescence. Cases in immunocompetent individuals have also been described. One hypothesis suggests that mucosal trauma may lead to persistent stimulation and activation of B-lymphocytes, resulting in transformation due to EBV persistence. Impaired EBV-specific cytotoxic T-cell response may allow for unchecked B-cell and natural killer/T-cell proliferation.2 Tirzepatide, used for weight loss and type 2 diabetes, is associated with gastrointestinal tract adverse effects, including nausea, vomiting, and reduced appetite. In this case, such effects may have contributed to transient immunosuppression, leading to EBVMCU.5The patient also reported occupational nitrous oxide exposure. Studies have shown that long-term nitrous oxide inhalation showed significantly higher levels of interferon-γ and IL-4 concentrations. Although not validated clinically, long-term nitrous oxide inhalation has been shown to alter immune function markers, potentially contributing to subclinical immunosuppression.6 Following discontinuation of tirzepatide, the ulcer showed progressive healing within 1 month. Oncology consultation led to supportive treatment for EBVMCU, and there has been no evidence of disease recurrence at 6-month follow-up. Early diagnosis of EBVMCU is crucial to distinguish it from aggressive lymphoproliferative malignant neoplasms and to avoid unnecessary treatments. EBVMCU generally follows an indolent course and may resolve spontaneously or with minimal intervention.7In contrast, cHL, oral lymphomas, and DLBCL require intensive therapy. A thorough clinical history—including immunosuppressive medications or immune-modulating agents, like tirzepatide—plays a key role in diagnosis. While symptom resolution followed drug cessation in this case, further research is needed to explore a definitive causal relationship.
